clue.text: Hero's foe encompasses evil in vain

indicators.note: the word for evil is placed in the middle of the word for vain, splitting it after its first letter

parts.note: taken as written
ill means evil, as in ill will

explanation.surface: The hero's enemy embodies wickedness, all to no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'encompasses' looks like the container signal but is a link: the villain embodies the wordplay. The container signal is 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: The antagonist who opposes a story's hero is its bad guy or blackguard.

parts.note: a pocket reference book named from Latin words meaning 'go with me', so it is a guide that accompanies its owner

explanation.surface: A guidebook that goes everywhere with me.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase behind the answer translates as 'go with me', which is what 'My accompanying' spells out.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin-derived term for a small reference manual carried about for constant consultation.

clue.text: Apprentice-ruler of old city in hiding.

parts.note: L is the learner plate sign, so an apprentice
Ur is the ancient city of Mesopotamia
a king is a ruler

explanation.surface: A trainee monarch of an ancient city is lying low.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in a different order from the clue: L, then UR, then KING; 'of' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying concealed in wait, as a predator does, is a synonym for being in hiding.

clue.text: Original pattern of cheap tyre construction

indicators.note: construction means the letters are built up into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: The prototype for how a budget tyre is built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'construction' rearranges the nine letters of CHEAP TYRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A prototype or model from which copies derive is its original pattern.

clue.text: There's no alternative to it when one's desperate

definitions.text: There's no alternative to it when one's desperate

parts.words: There's no alternative to it when one's desperate
parts.note: refers to the phrase 'X or nothing', the reckless all-out venture where the only other option is nothing at all

explanation.surface: Something a desperate person must go for, having no other option.
explanation.walkthrough: The old expression 'neck or nothing' describes a do-or-die attempt: nothing is the only alternative.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'neck or nothing' pairs the body part with nothing as the sole other choice in a desperate gamble.

parts.note: Lord's is the London cricket ground, whose stumps-and-bails sets are named after small gates

explanation.surface: The gates of heaven, belonging to God.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Lord's' looks religious, but Lord's is a cricket ground in London; the answer once meant small gates and now names the stumps cricketers bowl at.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket's stumps took their name from the small gate or wicket, so at Lord's cricket ground these are the gates.

clue.text: No peace for large church in Wilts

definitions.note: a place in Wilts, the short form of Wiltshire

parts.note: war is the absence of peace
a minster is a large or important church

explanation.surface: No tranquillity for a cathedral in Wiltshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilts is the abbreviation of Wiltshire, a county in south-west England; the answer is a town there.
explanation.definitionFit: This market town lies in western Wiltshire, so it is a place in Wilts.

parts.note: the cast is the group of actors in a play
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: Theatrical company jots down a class of society.
explanation.definitionFit: A hereditary class in a rigid social hierarchy, as in India.

explanation.surface: A written publication creates an effect.
explanation.definitionFit: Each issue of a book is a printing run, and a printing run is also called an impression.

indicators.note: being on board a ship means being inside it, so the word for stop goes inside the ship's letters

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, the vessel boarded
to end is to stop

explanation.surface: Messages telling someone to halt while aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' is the old convention for being aboard a steamship, so the stop sits within the ship's two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispatch something is to send it off; both verbs in the third person.

clue.text: Order Greek doctor to take care of one perhaps

indicators.note: taking care of something means holding it safe, so the doctor's word encloses the other piece

parts.note: RI is Rhode Island, one of the US states, the 'perhaps' showing it is an example

explanation.surface: A command telling a Greek physician to look after a patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a verb, but the definition is a Greek order of architecture. 'one perhaps' is one of the states, RI.
explanation.definitionFit: The plainest of the classical column styles, originating in ancient Greece.

explanation.surface: A Danish prince making a journey to a shrine.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten kings of Denmark bore the name; it is also the pilgrim hero of Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: A regnal name of many Danish kings, and the traveller of Bunyan's allegory.

explanation.surface: Sent off in a padded envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is armoured: wearing chain mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Sent by post, and clad in chain armour that protects the body.

parts.note: nine is the number just below ten
ties are knots

explanation.surface: A ship doing less than ten knots is behaving badly.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the phrase 'the Naughty Nineties', the 1890s; 'making' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1890s are known as the Naughty decade, so the word completes that fixed phrase.

clue.text: Universal liberty sometimes means a fight

explanation.surface: Freedom for everyone can lead to a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, freedom granted to everyone; idiomatically, a disorderly brawl in which anyone joins.

parts.note: CA is a chartered accountant
gey is a Scots word for very

explanation.surface: A tight-lipped bookkeeper who is very Scottish.
explanation.definitionFit: Being guarded and unwilling to reveal information.

explanation.surface: Remain in one's house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' is a link between the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A period of living somewhere, as in a writer's stay at a college, and also the dwelling itself.

clue.text: Tick off gown at reduced price

explanation.surface: Scold someone about a discounted frock.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is literal: a dress marked down in price.
explanation.definitionFit: To reprimand severely, and read literally a frock whose price has come down.

clue.text: What on earth's the point of getting agitated ?

definitions.text: What on earth's the point of getting agitated ?

parts.words: What on earth's the point of getting agitated ?
parts.note: read literally, the place on the earth's surface directly above where the ground starts shaking in a quake

explanation.surface: An exasperated question: why bother getting worked up?
explanation.walkthrough: 'What on earth's the point' sounds exasperated, but asks literally for the point on the earth above an earthquake's agitation.
explanation.definitionFit: The surface point directly above an earthquake's focus, where the ground is shaken most.

clue.text: A creature a thousand feet down (for a spell)

parts.note: mille is Latin for a thousand
pede is from the Latin for feet

explanation.surface: An animal a thousand feet below ground, briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down (for a spell)' says the name is written down in its spelt form: Latin for a thousand plus feet; 'spell' tempts as a period of time but means spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A many-legged arthropod, a creature whose name claims a thousand legs.

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A sign saying a property is available is a modest claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges TO LET plus IS.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech that understates by negating the opposite, as in 'not bad'.

clue.text: The latest thing in ballades. French style

definitions.text: The latest thing in ballades. French style

parts.words: The latest thing in ballades. French style
parts.note: the closing short stanza of a ballade, named with a French word

explanation.surface: Fashion news: the newest trend in songs, Paris-style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The latest thing' sounds like fashion but means the final part: the short last stanza of a ballade, a French verse form.
explanation.definitionFit: The short concluding stanza of a ballade, addressing a patron, takes this French name.

clue.text: Having fierce force and point in colour

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the word for the colour

parts.note: violet is a colour
N, north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Something with intense strength and a sharp tip in a bright hue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point' is a compass point, N, put 'in' VIOLET; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with great physical force or intensity, as a storm does.

clue.text: People about to back symbolic system

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the people's word goes round the other piece

parts.note: a nation is a people

indicators.note: back means the little word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A people about to return to a symbol-based scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns TO into OT, and NATION goes 'about' it: N-OT-ATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of written symbols representing, for example, music or mathematics.

indicators.note: turns means the combined letters are read from end to start

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a graduate
wan means pale

explanation.surface: An oriental ruler makes a university leaver go white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses BA + WAN as a single run.
explanation.definitionFit: A Muslim ruler or governor in India under the Mughals.

parts.note: a famous composer, a writer of musical notes, whose best-known song is the farewell 'Good-bye'; vale is Latin for farewell

explanation.surface: A celebrated author describing a valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vale' looks like a valley but is the Latin farewell; 'Noted' means using musical notes. The Italian song composer wrote 'Good-bye!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Paolo Tosti, the Italian-born composer, wrote the popular song 'Good-bye!', a farewell.

parts.note: Jane Shore was the mistress of King Edward IV

explanation.surface: A woman from history is left stranded.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Shore was a famous mistress of the English king Edward IV.
explanation.definitionFit: A beached boat is aground on land, so it is stranded.

parts.note: a dam is an animal mother

explanation.surface: A mother who designs buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Adam was the Scottish neoclassical architect; 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Adam, the eighteenth-century Scottish designer of houses and interiors.

indicators.note: wild means the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Gales that put up a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges WINDS THAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold out against something is to resist it.

clue.text: Previous century would make this open secret

indicators.note: the century letter would come before this word, so it is taken away from the front of the secret word

parts.note: covert means secret
C is a hundred, a century

explanation.surface: An earlier age would turn this into a hidden matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Put C (century) previous to, that is before, this answer and it becomes COVERT, secret; 'would make this' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Done openly and not concealed.

indicators.note: a mess means the letters are jumbled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
the word stable, its 's meaning is

explanation.surface: A stable that is filthy and disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' rearranges I (one) and STABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Like an animal, savage or depraved.

clue.text: Take position for driving a sea-beast

parts.note: to man a post is to take up position there
taken as written
in golf the ball is driven from a tee

explanation.surface: Getting into position to drive a sea creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'driving' is golf: a TEE is the peg a ball is driven from.
explanation.definitionFit: A large aquatic herbivore, the sea cow.
